# Additions to Esther — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Multiple authors; Greek additions composed c. 100–50 BCE; one addition signed by "Lysimachus of Jerusalem" |
| **Date** | Greek additions added to the Hebrew Esther between 114 BCE and 50 BCE |
| **Audience** | Greek-reading Jews in the Diaspora |
| **Genre** | Narrative expansion; liturgical prayer; royal decree (in part, parody) |
| **Timeline** | Set in the Persian court of Ahasuerus (Xerxes), c. 480 BCE |
| **In One Sentence** | Six additions to the Greek Esther supply what the Hebrew book conspicuously lacks — explicit prayers to God, a divine dream, royal letters, and an agonized Esther whose obedience to her king is purchased at terrible personal cost — transforming a secular court tale into an explicitly theological narrative about divine providence and faithful Jewish identity. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Hebrew Book of Esther is one of the most unusual texts in the entire Hebrew Bible. God is never mentioned. Prayer is never mentioned. Torah is never mentioned. The people of Israel are never called God's people. Esther marries a Persian king, participates in a Persian royal harem, and nowhere in the book does any character call upon God for help, offer a prayer, or acknowledge divine intervention. The book is a virtuoso piece of literary suspense and irony — but it is, theologically speaking, conspicuously silent about the very things that the rest of the Hebrew Bible never stops talking about.

This theological silence was noticed and felt in the ancient world. The rabbis debated the book's canonical status partly on these grounds. The text that circulated in Greek among Diaspora Jewish communities was, apparently, not silent in the same way — or at least, translators and adapters decided it should not be. The Greek Esther, as transmitted in the Septuagint, includes six substantial additions (labeled A through F by modern scholars, following the ordering established by the scholar C.C. Torrey in the early twentieth century) that together add 107 verses to the book's original 167 Hebrew verses, increasing the text by more than sixty percent.

These additions were composed at different times and possibly by different authors. Addition F includes a colophon (a scribal note) identifying "Lysimachus, son of Ptolemy, of Jerusalem" as the translator/adapter who brought the text to Egypt "in the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra" — a date that has been variously identified as 114 BCE or 77 BCE. This makes the Greek Esther additions among the most precisely dateable texts in the deuterocanonical corpus. The additions were clearly designed not merely to translate the Hebrew but to transform it — to give the book the theological content that Greek-reading Jewish communities expected a sacred text to contain.

The world behind these additions is the world of Diaspora Judaism under ongoing pressure: Jews living at courts, in cities, in cultural environments that were simultaneously seductive and threatening. The additions make explicit what the Hebrew text left implicit: that Esther is not simply a clever woman navigating a dangerous court, but a faithful Jew who fears God, abhors her situation, and survives only through divine intervention. The additions resolve the Hebrew text's theological ambiguity by importing theological certainty.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The six additions serve three distinct functions, and understanding those functions illuminates why the text was expanded in the way it was.

The first function is theological legitimation. Additions A and F (the dream of Mordecai and its interpretation) frame the entire narrative as divine providence: what follows is not coincidence or human cleverness but the unfolding of a dream God gave to Mordecai. The dream, with its imagery of two dragons (Mordecai and Haman), a roaring river (Haman's power), and a tiny spring that becomes a great flood (Esther), maps the story onto apocalyptic symbolic imagery and explicitly places it within God's sovereign plan. The final interpretation in Addition F makes the point unmissable: "God did all these things, which are his signs and wonders" (F:1). The Hebrew Esther's silence about God is retroactively filled.

The second function is pietistic intensification. Additions C — the prayers of Mordecai and Esther — are the theological and emotional heart of the entire Greek Esther. Mordecai's prayer (C:1–11) is a formal petition acknowledging God's sovereignty, confessing that he refused to bow to Haman not out of arrogance but out of devotion to God alone. Esther's prayer (C:12–30) is considerably longer, considerably more intimate, and considerably more anguished. Esther confesses her horror at her own situation: she abhors the bed of the uncircumcised man, she has not eaten at Haman's table, she hates the crown on her head as she would hate a menstrual cloth. The prayer reveals a character utterly unlike the composed, strategic Esther of the Hebrew text — this Esther is terrified, self-doubting, throwing herself on God's mercy because she has nowhere else to go. The prayer transforms her from a savvy court operator into a figure of genuine spiritual depth.

The third function is narrative elaboration. Additions B and E are the texts of Haman's decree and Artaxerxes' counter-decree — formal bureaucratic documents written in the elaborate style of Hellenistic royal correspondence. These additions give the narrative a kind of documentary weight: we see the official language of the empire that threatened Jewish existence, and we see the official language of its reversal. The additions also, unmistakably, satirize the pretensions of imperial administration: Haman's decree is so self-aggrandizing, so obviously written by a man in love with his own power, that it functions as a comic portrait of bureaucratic evil.

---

## How to Read This Book

The best way to read the Additions to Esther is to read the full Greek Esther — the Septuagint version — rather than attempting to read the additions in isolation. Modern study Bibles that present the Hebrew Esther followed by six disconnected additions give a misleading impression of the text; what was transmitted in Greek was a unified narrative, and the additions were designed to be read within that narrative.

If reading the additions in isolation, the order should follow Jerome's NRSV-style lettering system (A-F), which reflects the dramatic sequence rather than the manuscript sequence (Jerome, finding the additions scattered through the Greek text, gathered them at the end of his Latin translation, which is why they appear at the end in Catholic Bibles). The sequence is: Addition A (Mordecai's dream, the plot against the king) — this sets the frame. Addition B (Haman's edict) — read this where it would fall in chapter 3 of Hebrew Esther, after 3:13. Addition C (prayers of Mordecai and Esther) — read this where it falls between chapters 4 and 5. Addition D (Esther approaches the king) — this replaces and expands Hebrew Esther 5:1–2. Addition E (Mordecai's edict) — read after Hebrew Esther 8:12. Addition F (interpretation of the dream, colophon) — the conclusion.

Addition D deserves particular attention. In the Hebrew text, Esther's approach to the king is dispatched in two verses: "On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace... When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight and he held out to her the golden scepter" (Esther 5:1–2). Brisk, understated, efficient. The Addition expands this to twenty-four verses of agonizing suspense: Esther, terrified and pale, leaning on her maids because her legs have failed her, approaching the throne room while the king sits on it like a lion, his golden splendor filling the room. Esther faints. God changes the king's heart. The king leaps from his throne, takes her in his arms, tells her she will not die, and calls her his sister. The scene is melodramatic — but it is also genuinely moving, and it transforms the emotional register of the entire narrative from court comedy to something approaching tragedy with a providential resolution.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

**Hebrew Esther (the foundation beneath every addition):** The additions cannot be understood except in relation to the Hebrew Esther they expand. The most important exercise a reader can undertake is to read both versions and ask: what has changed? What theological moves has the addition made that the Hebrew text refused to make? Why might that refusal have been deliberate on the Hebrew author's part — and why did the Greek adapters find it insufficient?

**Judith (court woman saves her people through cleverness and courage):** The structural parallels between Esther and Judith are extensive (see the Judith Reader's Guide), but the Additions to Esther bring the two texts even closer together: both books, in their full forms, feature women who pray before their dangerous acts, women whose beauty is explicitly a weapon in service of God's purposes, women who abhor the compromises their situations have required. Judith's prayer before beheading Holofernes (Judith 9) and Esther's prayer before approaching the king (Addition C) are the emotional parallels of two women alone with God before everything is decided.

**Daniel (Diaspora court tales):** The Book of Daniel belongs to the genre of "court tale" along with the Hebrew Esther: stories of Jews navigating foreign imperial courts, maintaining their Jewish identity under pressure, and surviving through wisdom and divine favor. The Additions to Esther push the Hebrew Esther firmly into Daniel's theological territory: explicit prayer, explicit divine intervention, explicit acknowledgment that survival is God's doing.

**Psalm 22 (the righteous one's prayer of anguish):** Esther's prayer in Addition C — desperate, self-aware about her own complicity in uncomfortable arrangements, addressed to a God who alone can save — echoes the structure of the great individual lament psalms, particularly Psalm 22 ("My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"). The pattern is: anguished address, statement of dire situation, recollection of God's past faithfulness, renewed plea. Esther's prayer follows this template.

**Daniel 2 and 4 (dream and interpretation as divine communication):** Mordecai's dream in Addition A and its interpretation in Addition F follow the same pattern as the dreams of Daniel and Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2 and 4: symbolic imagery (dragons, rivers, a small spring becoming great waters) followed by deferred interpretation at the narrative's end. The technique frames the entire Esther narrative as dream-fulfillment, placing it within the apocalyptic framework that Daniel established.

**The Purim liturgical tradition:** The Hebrew Book of Esther is explicitly a Purim text — it explains the origin of the festival (Esther 9) and was read publicly in synagogue on Purim. The Greek Esther, with its additions, was used in Hellenistic Jewish communities who may have had different or less developed Purim practices. The additions' explicit theological content made the text suitable for communities that needed the story to carry more explicit theological freight.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The most important thing a modern reader might miss is that the additions were not written to deceive anyone into thinking the Hebrew Esther said things it did not say. Ancient readers who had access to both the Hebrew and Greek texts would have known the difference. The additions were a legitimate form of interpretive expansion — midrash in Greek dress — that made the theological subtext of the Hebrew text explicit. The question the additions are answering is: given that we believe God saves his people through historical events, and given that this story is clearly about God saving his people, why doesn't the Hebrew text say so? The additions answer: here is what the story always meant.

Esther's statement in her prayer that she abhors "the bed of the uncircumcised" (Addition C, v. 26) is one of the most startling admissions in the entire deuterocanonical corpus. The Hebrew Esther presents Esther's marriage to Ahasuerus with no indication that it is a problem; she sleeps with the king, she becomes queen, she navigates the court with consummate skill. The Greek addition does not pretend this isn't complicated. Esther's prayer acknowledges that her life has required compromises that she finds spiritually repugnant, and she asks God to understand and forgive. This is a more honest and more humanly complex portrait than either the Hebrew text's silence or a simple reading that presents Esther as simply faithful. The addition treats Esther as a real person in a genuinely difficult situation, not a religious ideal.

The colophon in Addition F — "Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, of Jerusalem, translated the foregoing letter about Purim and said that it was genuine, and that Dositheus, who said that he was a priest and Levite, and his son Ptolemy brought it" — is one of the few places in the entire Old Testament/deuterocanonical corpus where we have something like a named translator and a delivery date. Scholars debate which Ptolemy and Cleopatra are meant (and therefore whether the date is 114 or 77 BCE), but the existence of this note at all is remarkable: it is a claim to authenticity, a kind of ancient certification that this is a real text with a real history. The author of the note clearly believed that provenance mattered.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The situation of the Additions to Esther is more complicated than most deuterocanonical texts because the text involved — Esther — is canonical in both the Hebrew Tanakh and all Christian Bibles. The question is not whether to include Esther but which Esther to include.

Jerome, when translating the Vulgate, noticed that the Greek Esther included substantial material not found in any Hebrew text he had access to. Rather than translate the additions within the narrative (as the Septuagint presented them), he gathered all the material lacking a Hebrew equivalent and placed it at the end of the book, with a note explaining what he had done. This is why Catholic Bibles have "Esther with the additions" but present the additions awkwardly, and why the additions are labeled A-F by modern scholars working to put them back in their original positions.

Protestant reformers, following the Hebrew canon principle, used only the Hebrew text of Esther and set aside the additions as Apocrypha. The result is that most Protestant Bibles contain the ten-chapter Hebrew Esther, while Catholic and Orthodox Bibles contain a significantly longer Greek Esther that is, theologically speaking, a substantially different reading experience.

The Roman Catholic Church defined the longer Greek Esther (with additions) as canonical at the Council of Trent (1546). The Eastern Orthodox tradition also treats the full Greek Esther as canonical. The NRSV includes the additions in its Apocrypha/deuterocanonical sections, helpfully labeled and placed in narrative sequence.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 480 BCE | Reign of Xerxes I (Ahasuerus) — the Persian king in the Esther narrative |
| c. 400–350 BCE | Probable composition of the Hebrew Book of Esther |
| c. 250–200 BCE | Septuagint translation of other Hebrew books; Esther likely translated later |
| c. 114 BCE | One proposed date for Lysimachus' delivery of the Greek Esther to Egypt (Addition F colophon) |
| c. 100 BCE | Greek Esther (with additions) in circulation |
| c. 77 BCE | Alternative proposed date for Lysimachus' delivery (if Ptolemy IX Soter II and Cleopatra III) |
| c. 90 CE | Jamnia discussions; Hebrew Esther's canonical status debated by rabbis |
| c. 382–405 CE | Jerome's Vulgate: gathers additions at end of Esther, notes their absence from Hebrew |
| 1546 CE | Council of Trent defines the full Greek Esther (with additions) as deuterocanonical for Roman Catholics |
| 1611 CE | King James Bible Apocrypha section includes the additions; Hebrew Esther in OT |
